rifling: (a) The act or process of making the grooves in a rifled cannon or gun barrel. (b) The system of grooves in a rifled gun barrel or cannon. Shunt rifling, rifling for cannon, in which one side of the groove is made deeper than the other, to facilitate loading with shot having projections which enter by the deeper part of the grooves.
riddling: Speaking in a riddle or riddles; containing a riddle. "Riddling triplets." Tennyson. -- Rid"dling, adv.
rightful: 1. Righteous; upright; just; good; -- said of persons. (old) Chaucer. 2. Consonant to justice; just; as, a rightful cause. 3. Having the right or just claim according to established laws; being or holding by right; as, the rightful heir to a throne or an estate; a rightful king. 4. Belonging, held, or possessed by right, or by just claim; as, a rightful inheritance;
rivage: 1. A bank, shore, or coast. (old) Spenser. From the green rivage many a fall Of diamond rillets musical. Tennyson. 2. (O.Eng.Law) A duty paid to the crown for the passage of vessels on certain rivers.
rinser: One who, or that which, rinses.
ricochet: A rebound or skipping, as of a ball along the ground when a gun is fired at a low angle of elevation, or of a fiat stone thrown along the surface of water. Ricochet firing (Mil.), the firing of guns… | To operate upon by ricochet firing. See Ricochet, n.
rivality: 1. Rivalry; competition. (old) 2. Equality, as of right or rank. (old) hak.
rit: 3d pers. ssing. pres. of Ride, contracted from rideth. Chaucer.
rigel: A fixed star of the first magnitude in the left foot of the constellation Orion. [Written also Regel.]
rigolette: A woman's light scarflike head covering, usually knit or crocheted of wool.
richweed: An herb (Pilea pumila) of the Nettle family, having a smooth, juicy, pellucid stem; -- called also clearweed.
rivered: Supplied with rivers; as, a well rivered country.
richness: The quality or state of being rich (in any sense of the adjective).
risquee: Hazardous; risky; esp., fig., verging upon impropriety; dangerously close to, or suggestive of, what is indecent or of doubtful morality; as, a risqué story. Henry Austin.
riffraff: Sweepings; refuse; the lowest order of society. Beau & Fl.
riprap: A foundation or sustaining wall of stones thrown together without order, as in deep water or on a soft bottom.
ripperact: An act or a bill conferring upon a chief executive, as a governor or mayor, large powers of appointment and removal of heads of departments or other subordinate officials. [Polit. Cant, U. S.]
rink: 1. The smooth and level extent of ice marked off for the game of curling. 2. An artificial sheet of ice, generally under cover, used for skating; also, a floor prepared for skating on with roller skates, or a building with such a floor.
risen: 1. p. p. & a. from Rise. "Her risen Son and Lord." Keble. 2. Obs. imp. pl. of Rise. Chaucer.
rimple: A fold or wrinkle. See Rumple.
riceshell: Any one of numerous species of small white polished marine shells of the genus Olivella.
rim: 1. The border, edge, or margin of a thing, usually of something circular or curving; as, the rim of a kettle or basin. 2. The lower part of the abdomen. (old) Shak. | To furnish with a rim; to border.
rigorist: One who is rigorous; -- sometimes applied to an extreme Jansenist.
ringarmature: An armature for a dynamo or motor having the conductors wound on a ring.
riotry: The act or practice of rioting; riot. "Electioneering riotry." Walpole.
rill: 1. A very small brook; a streamlet. 2. (Astron.) See Rille.
rivery: Having rivers; as, a rivery country. Drayton.
rickety: 1. Affected with rickets. 2. Feeble in the joints; imperfect; weak; shaky.
risker: One who risks or hazards. Hudibras.
ritualism: 1. A system founded upon a ritual or prescribed form of religious worship; adherence to, or observance of, a ritual. 2. Specifically :(a) The principles and practices of those in the Church of England, who in the development of the Oxford movement, so- called, have insisted upon a return to the use in church services of the symbolic ornaments (altar cloths, encharistic…
ridotto: A favorite Italian public entertainment, consisting of music and dancing, -- held generally on fast eves. Brande & C. There are to be ridottos at guinea tickets. Walpole. | To hold ridottos. J. G. Cooper.
ribald: A low, vulgar, brutal, foul-mouthed wretch; a lewd fellow. Spenser. Pope. Ribald was almost a class name in the feudal system . . . He was his patron's parasite, bulldog, and tool . . . | Low; base; mean; filthy; obscene. The busy day, Waked by the lark, hath roused the ribald crows. Shak.
rippingpanel: A long patch, on a balloon, to be ripped off, by the rip cord, at landing, in order to allow the immediate escape of gas and instant deflation of the bag.
river: 1. A large stream of water flowing in a bed or channel and emptying into the ocean, a sea, a lake, or another stream; a stream larger than a rivulet or brook. Transparent and sparkling rivers, from… | To hawk by the side of a river; to fly hawks at river fowl. (old) Halliwell.
rite: The act of performing divine or solemn service, as established by law, precept, or custom; a formal act of religion or other solemn duty; a solemn observance; a ceremony; as, the rites of freemasonry. He looked with indifference on rites, names, and forms of ecclesiastical polity. Macaulay. Syn. -- Form; ceremony; observance; ordinance.
ring: 1. To cause to sound, especially by striking, as a metallic body; as, to ring a bell. 2. To make (a sound), as by ringing a bell; to sound. The shard-borne beetle, with his drowsy hums, Hath rung… | 1. To sound, as a bell or other sonorous body, particularly a metallic one. Now ringen trompes loud and clarion. Chaucer. Why ring not out the bells Shak. 2. To practice making music with bells.
rimose: 1. Full of rimes, fissures, or chinks. 2. (Nat. Hist.) Having long and nearly parallel clefts or chinks, like those in the bark of trees.
rideau: A small mound of earth; ground slightly elevated; a small ridge.
righter: One who sets right; one who does justice or redresses wrong. Shelton.
ringlet: 1. A small ring; a small circle; specifically, a fairy ring. You demi-puppets, that By moonshine do the green sour ringlets make, Whereof the ewe not bites. Shak. 2. A curl; especially, a curl of hair. [Her golden tresses] in wanton ringlets waved. Milton.
ribbonism: The principles and practices of the Ribbonmen. See Ribbon Society, under Ribbon.
rightlined: Formed by right lines; rectilineal; as, a right-lined angle.
ridge: 1. The back, or top of the back; a crest. Hudibras. 2. A range of hills or mountains, or the upper part of such a range; any extended elevation between valleys. "The frozen ridges of the Alps." Shak. | 1. To form a ridge of; to furnish with a ridge or ridges; to make into a ridge or ridges. Bristles ranged like those that ridge the back Of chafed wild boars. Milton. 2.
ringleader: 1. The leader of a circle of dancers; hence, the leader of a number of persons acting together; the leader of a herd of animals. A primacy of order, such an one as the ringleader hath in a dance. Barrow. 2. Opprobriously, a leader of a body of men engaged in the violation of law or in an illegal enterprise, as rioters, mutineers, or the like.
righteous: Doing, or according with, that which is right; yielding to all their due; just; equitable; especially, free from wrong, guilt, or sin; holy; as, a righteous man or act; a righteous retribution. Fearless in his righteous cause. Milton. Syn. -- Upright; just; godly; holy; uncorrupt; virtuous; honest; equitable; rightful.
ripper: One who brings fish from the seacoast to markets in inland towns. (old) But what's the action we are for now Robbing a ripper of his fish. Beau & Fl. | 1. One who, or that which, rips; a ripping tool. 2. A tool for trimming the edges of roofing slates. 3. Anything huge, extreme, startling, etc. [Slang.]
rightabout: A turning directly about by the right, so as to face in the opposite direction; also, the quarter directly opposite; as, to turn to the right-about. To send to the right-about, to cause to turn toward the opposite point or quarter; -- hence, of troops, to cause to turn and retreat. [Colloq.] Sir W. Scott.
ringtailed: Having the tail crossed by conspicuous bands of color. Ring- tailed cat (Zoöl.), the cacomixle. -- Ring-tailed eagle (Zoöl.), a young golden eagle.
ripcord: A cord by which the gas bag of a balloon may be ripped open for a limited distance to release the gas quickly and so cause immediate descent.
rightwiseness: Righteousness. (old) In doom and eke in rightwisnesse. Chaucer.
ritualistic: Pertaining to, or in accordance with, a ritual; adhering to ritualism.
rift: 1. An opening made by riving or splitting; a cleft; a fissure. Spenser. 2. A shallow place in a stream; a ford. | To cleave; to rive; to split; as, to rift an oak or a rock; to rift the clouds. Longfellow. To dwell these rifted rocks between. Wordsworth.
riotise: Excess; tumult; revelry. (old) His life he led in lawless riotise. Spenser.
rivet: A metallic pin with a head, used for uniting two plates or pieces of material together, by passing it through them and then beating or pressing down the point so that it shall spread out and form a… | 1. To fasten with a rivet, or with rivets; as, to rivet two pieces of iron. 2. To spread out the end or point of, as of a metallic pin, rod, or bolt, by beating or pressing, so as to form a sort of…
ridiculosity: The quality or state of being ridiculous; ridiculousness; also, something ridiculous. (old) Bailey.
rivulet: A small stream or brook; a streamlet. By fountain or by shady rivulet He sought them. Milton.
rigging: DRess; tackle; especially (Naut.), the ropes, chains, etc., that support the masts and spars of a vessel, and serve as purchases for adjusting the sails, etc. See Illustr. of Ship and Sails. Running rigging (Naut.), all those ropes used in bracing the yards, making and shortening sail, etc., such as braces, sheets, halyards, clew lines, and the like.
riband: See Ribbon. Riband jasper (Min.), a variety of jasper having stripes of different colors, as red and green.
ringlestone: The ringed dotterel, or ring plover. [Prov.Eng.]
rigorous: 1. Manifesting, exercising, or favoring rigor; allowing no abatement or mitigation; scrupulously accurate; exact; strict; severe; relentless; as, a rigorous officer of justice; a rigorous execution of law; a rigorous definition or demonstration. He shall be thrown down the Tarpeian Rock With rigorous hands. Shak.
ripen: 1. To grow ripe; to become mature, as grain, fruit, flowers, and the like; as, grapes ripen in the sun. 2. To approach or come to perfection. | 1. To cause to mature; to make ripe; as, the warm days ripened the corn. 2. To mature; to fit or prepare; to bring to perfection; as, to ripen the judgment. When faith and love, which parted from…
ripely: Maturely; at the fit time. Shak.
ricker: A stout pole for use in making a rick, or for a spar to a boat.
rivel: To contract into wrinkles; to shrivel; to shrink; as, riveled fruit; riveled flowers. (old) Pope. "Riveled parchments." Walpole. | A wrinkle; a rimple. (old) Holland.
rise: 1. To move from a lower position to a higher; to ascend; to mount up. Specifically: -- (a) To go upward by walking, climbing, flying, or any other voluntary motion; as, a bird rises in the air; | 1. The act of rising, or the state of being risen. 2. The distance through which anything rises; as, the rise of the thermometer was ten degrees; the rise of the river was six feet;
riveting: 1. The act of joining with rivets; the act of spreading out and clinching the end, as of a rivet, by beating or pressing. 2. The whole set of rivets, collectively. Tomlinsin. Butt riveting, riveting in which the ends or edges of plates form a butt joint, and are fastened together by being riveted to a narrow strip which covers the joint.
ringneck: 1. (Zoöl.) Any one of several species of small plovers of the genus Ægialitis, having a ring around the neck. The ring is black in summer, but becomes brown or gray in winter. The semipalmated plover (Æ. semipalmata) and the piping plover (Æ. meloda) are common North American species. Called also ring plover, and ring-necked plover. 2. (Zoöl.) The ring-necked duck.
riddance: 1. The act of ridding or freeing; deliverance; a cleaning up or out. Thou shalt not make clean riddance of the corners of thy field. Lev. xxiii. 22. 2. The state of being rid or free; freedom; escape. "Riddance from all adversity." Hooker.
riparian: Of or pertaining to the bank of a river; as, riparian rights.
rive: To rend asunder by force; to split; to cleave; as, to rive timber for rails or shingles. I shall ryve him through the sides twain. Chaucer. The scolding winds have rived the knotty oaks. Shak. | To be split or rent asunder. Freestone rives, splits, and breaks in any direction. Woodward.
righthearted: Having a right heart or disposition. -- Right"-heart`ed*ness, n.
ritardando: Retarding; -- a direction for slower time; rallentado.
riffle: A trough or sluice having cleats, grooves, or steps across the bottom for holding quicksilver and catching particles of gold when auriferous earth is washed; also, one of the cleats, grooves, or steps in such a trough. Also called ripple.
rifle: 1. To seize and bear away by force; to snatch away; to carry off. Till time shall rifle every youthful grace. Pope. 2. To strip; to rob; to pillage. Piers Plowman. | 1. To raffle. (old) Chapman. 2. To commit robbery. Bp. Hall.
righteously: In a righteous manner; as, to judge righteously.
rixatrix: A scolding or quarrelsome woman; a scold. Burrill.
rickstand: A flooring or framework on which a rick is made.
riparious: Growing along the banks of rivers; riparian.
ricinine: A bitter white crystalline alkaloid extracted from the seeds of the castor-oil plant.
rip: 1. To divide or separate the parts of, by cutting or tearing; to tear or cut open or off; to tear off or out by violence; as, to rip a garment by cutting the stitches; to rip off the skin of a beast; | 1. A rent made by ripping, esp. by a seam giving way; a tear; a place torn; laceration. 2. Etym: [Perh. a corruption of the first syllable of reprobate.] A term applied to a mean, worthless thing or…
ringhead: An instrument used for stretching woolen cloth.
rime: A rent or long aperture; a chink; a fissure; a crack. Sir T. Browne. | White frost; hoarfrost; congealed dew or vapor. The trees were now covered with rime. De Quincey.
ritornello: (a) A short return or repetition; a concluding symphony to an air, often consisting of the burden of the song. (a) A short intermediate symphony, or instrumental passage, in the course of a vocal piece; an interlude.
ribbonwood: A malvaceous tree (Hoheria populnea) of New Zealand, the bark of which is used for cordage.
ringstraked: Ring-streaked. Cattle ringstraked, speckled, and spotted. Gen. xxx. 39.
ringbone: A morbid growth or deposit of bony matter between or on the small pastern and the great pastern bones. J. H. Walsh.
rioter: 1. One who riots; a reveler; a roisterer. Chaucer. 2. (Law) One who engages in a riot. See Riot, n., 3.
ringbolt: An eyebolt having a ring through the eye.
rigid: 1. Firm; stiff; unyielding; not pliant; not flexible. Upright beams innumerable Of rigid spears. Milton. 2. Hence, not lax or indulgent; severe; inflexible; strict; as, a rigid father or master; rigid discipline; rigid criticism; a rigid sentence. The more rigid order of principles in religion and government. Hawthorne. Syn. -- Stiff; unpliant; inflexible; unyielding; strict;
riksdaler: A Swedish coin worth about twenty-seven cents. It was formerly the unit of value in Sweden.
ricinus: A genus of plants of the Spurge family, containing but one species (R. communis), the castor-oil plant. The fruit is three- celled, and contains three large seeds from which castor oil iss expressed. See Palma Christi.
rick: A stack or pile, as of grain, straw, or hay, in the open air, usually protected from wet with thatching. Golden clusters of beehive ricks, rising at intervals beyond the hedgerows. G. Eliot. | To heap up in ricks, as hay, etc.
rimmer: An implement for cutting, trimming, or ornamenting the rim of anything, as the edges of pies, etc.; also, a reamer. Knight.
righthand: 1. Situated or being on the right; nearer the right hand than the left; as, the right-hand side, room, or road. 2. Chiefly relied on; almost indispensable. Mr. Alexander Truncheon, who is their right-hand man in the troop. Addison. Right-hand rope, a rope which is laid up and twisted with the sun, that is, in the same direction as plain-laid rope. See Illust. of Cordage.
rising: 1. Attaining a higher place; taking, or moving in, an upward direction; appearing above the horizon; ascending; as, the rising moon. 2. Increasing in wealth, power, or distinction; | More than; exceeding; upwards of; as, a horse rising six years of age. [Colloq. & Low, U.S.]
rigsdaler: A Danish coin worth about fifty-four cents. It was former unit of value in Denmark.
righthandedness: The state or quality of being right-handed; hence, skill; dexterity.
rightminded: Having a right or honest mind. -- Right"-mind`ed*ness, n.
richesse: Wealth; riches. See the Note under Riches. (old) Some man desireth for to have richesse. Chaucer. The richesse of all heavenly grace. Spenser.
rimer: A tool for shaping the rimes of a ladder.
rigidulous: Somewhat rigid or stiff; as, a rigidulous bristle.
ridder: One who, or that which, rids.
ringtoss: A game in which the object is to toss a ring so that it will catch upon an upright stick.
rigorism: 1. Rigidity in principle or practice; strictness; -- opposed to laxity. 2. Severity, as of style, or the like. Jefferson.
ripsaw: A handsaw with coarse teeth which have but a slight set, used for cutting wood in the direction of the fiber; -- called also ripping saw.
ripienist: A player in the ripieno portion of an orchestra. See Ripieno.
riding: One of the three jurisdictions into which the county of York, in England, is divided; -- formerly under the government of reeve. They are called the North, the East, and the West, Riding. Blackstone. | 1. Employed to travel; traveling; as, a riding clerk. "One riding apparitor." Ayliffe. 2. Used for riding on; as, a riding horse. 3. Used for riding, or when riding; devoted to riding;
ripeness: The state or quality of being ripe; maturity;; completeness; perfection; as, the ripeness of grain; ripeness of manhood; ripeness of judgment. Time, which made them their fame outlive, To Cowley scarce did ripeness give. Denham.
rimaudahan: The clouded tiger cat (Felis marmorata) of Southern Asia and the East Indies.
rig: 1. To furnish with apparatus or gear; to fit with tackling. 2. To dress; to equip; to clothe, especially in an odd or fanciful manner; -- commonly followed by out. | 1. (Naut.) The peculiar fitting in shape, number, and arrangement of sails and masts, by which different types of vessels are distinguished; as, schooner rig, ship rig, etc.
ringstreaked: Having circular streaks or lines on the body; as, ring-streaked goats.
rimey: To compose in rhyme; to versify. (old) [Lays] rimeyed in their first Breton tongue. Chaucer.
ridgepole: The timber forming the ridge of a roof, into which the rafters are secured.
right: 1. Straight; direct; not crooked; as, a right line. "Right as any line." Chaucer 2. Upright; erect from a base; having an upright axis; not oblique; as, right ascension; a right pyramid or cone. 3. | 1. In a right manner. 2. In a right or straight line; directly; hence; straightway; immediately; next; as, he stood right before me; it went right to the mark; he came right out;
ricinic: Pertaining to, or derived from, castor oil; formerly, designating an acid now called ricinoleic acid.
ricinoleic: Pertaining to, or designating, a fatty acid analogous to oleic acid, obtained from castor oil as an oily substance, Cricinolic.
riser: 1. One who rises; as, an early riser. 2. (Arch.) (a) The upright piece of a step, from tread to tread. Hence: (b) Any small upright face, as of a seat, platform, veranda, or the like. 3. (Mining) A shaft excavated from below upward. 4. (Founding) A feed head. See under Feed, n.
ripidolite: A translucent mineral of a green color and micaceous structure, belonging to the chlorite group; a hydrous silicate of alumina, magnesia, and iron; -- called also clinochlore.
riot: 1. Wanton or unrestrained behavior; uproar; tumult. His headstrong riot hath no curb. Shak. 2. Excessive and exxpensive feasting; wild and loose festivity; revelry. Venus loveth riot and dispense. | 1. To engage in riot; to act in an unrestrained or wanton manner; to indulge in excess of luxury, feasting, or the like; to revel; to run riot; to go to excess. Now he exact of all, wastes in…
ringdove: A European wild pigeon (Columba palumbus) having a white crescent on each side of the neck, whence the name. Called also wood pigeon, and cushat.
ripe: 1. Ready for reaping or gathering; having attained perfection; mature; -- said of fruits, seeds, etc.; as, ripe grain. So mayst thou live, till, like ripe fruit, thou drop Into thy mother's lap. | To mature; to ripen. (old) Shak.
rivalry: The act of rivaling, or the state of being a rival; a competition. "Keen contention and eager rivalries." Jeffrey. Syn. -- Emulation; competition. See Emulation.
riffler: A curved file used in carving wool and marble.
righten: To do justice to. (old) Relieve [marginal reading, righten] the opressed. Isa. i. 17.
rial: A Spanish coin. See Real. (old) | A gold coin formerly current in England, of the value of ten shillings sterling in the reign of Henry VI., and of fifteen shillings in the reign of Elizabeth. [Spelt also ryal.] Brande & C.
riddler: One who riddles (grain, sand, etc.). | One who speaks in, or propounds, riddles.
ripler: One who brings fish from the seacoast to markets in inland towns. (old) But what's the action we are for now Robbing a ripper of his fish. Beau & Fl.
riden: imp. pl. & p. p. of Ride. Chaucer.
ric: A suffix signifying dominion, jurisdiction; as, bishopric, the district over which a bishop exercises authority.
ribbonman: A member of the Ribbon Society. See Ribbon Society, under Ribbon.
rightfulness: 1. The quality or state of being rightful; accordance with right and justice. 2. Moral rectitude; righteousness. (old) Wyclif. We fail of perfect rightfulness. Sir P. Sidney.
riverhood: The quality or state of being a river. "Useful riverhood." H. Miller.
ridiculize: To make ridiculous; to ridicule. (old) Chapman.
ricinolein: The glycerin salt of ricinoleic acid, occuring as a characteristic constituent of castor oil; -- formerly called palmin.
ribible: A small threestringed viol; a rebec. Moore (Encyc. of Music). All can be play on gittern or ribible. Chaucer.
ringtail: 1. (Zoöl.) A bird having a distinct band of color across the tail, as the hen harrier. 2. (Naut.) A light sail set abaft and beyong the leech of a boom-and-gaff sail; -- called also ringsail. Ringtail boom (Naut.), a spar which is rigged on a boom for setting a ringtail.
riddle: 1. A sieve with coarse meshes, usually of wire, for separating coarser materials from finer, as chaff from grain, cinders from ashes, or gravel from sand. 2. A board having a row of pins, set zigzag,… | 1. To separate, as grain from the chaff, with a riddle; to pass through a riddle; as, riddle wheat; to riddle coal or gravel. 2. To perforate so as to make like a riddle; to make many holes in;
rigidness: The quality or state of being rigid.
risible: 1. Having the faculty or power of laughing; disposed to laugh. Laughing is our busines, . . . it has been made the definition of man that he is risible. Dr. H. More. 2. Exciting laughter; worthy to be laughed at; amusing. "Risible absurdities." Johnson. I hope you find nothing risible in my complaisance. Sir W. Scott. 3. Used in, or expressing, laughter; as, risible muscles.
ripply: Having ripples; as, ripply water; hence, resembling the sound of rippling water; as, ripply laughter; a ripply cove. Keats.
riggish: Like a rig or wanton. (old) "Riggish and unmaidenly." Bp. Hall.
ritual: Of or pertaining to rites or ritual; as, ritual service or sacrifices; the ritual law. | 1. A prescribed form of performing divine service in a particular church or communion; as, the Jewish ritual. 2. Hence, the code of ceremonies observed by an organization;
rinse: 1. To wash lightly; to cleanse with a second or repeated application of water after washing. 2. To cleancse by the introduction of water; -- applied especially to hollow vessels; as, to rinse a bottle. "Like a glass did break i' the rinsing." Shak.
rigadoon: A gay, lively dance for one couple, -- said to have been borrowed from Provence in France. W. Irving. Whose dancing dogs in rigadoons excel. Wolcott.
ribbed: 1. Furnished or formed with ribs; as, a ribbed cylinder; ribbed cloth. 2. (Mining) Intercalated with slate; -- said of a seam of coal. Raymond.
rinderpest: A highly contagious distemper or murrain, affecting neat cattle, and less commonly sheep and goats; -- called also cattle plague, Russian cattle plague, and steppe murrain.
ricinoleate: A salt of ricinoleic acid; -- formerly called palmate.
ribaudequin: 1. An engine of war used in the Middle Ages, consisting of a protected elevated staging on wheels, and armed in front with pikes. It was (after the 14th century) furnished with small cannon. 2. A huge bow fixed on the wall of a fortified town for casting javelins.
rizzar: To dry in the sun; as, rizzared haddock. [Scot.]
riotous: 1. Involving, or engaging in, riot; wanton; unrestrained; luxurious. The younger son . . . took his journey into a far country, and there wasted his substance with riotous living. Luke xv. 13. 2. Partaking of the nature of an unlawful assembly or its acts; seditious. -- Ri"ot*ous*ly, adv. -- Ri"ot*ous*ness, n.
ribes: A genus of shrubs including gooseberries and currants of many kinds.
rimfire: Having the percussion fulminate in a rim surrounding the base, distinguished from center-fire; -- said of cartridges; also, using rim-fire cartridges; as, a rim-fire gun. Such cartridges are now little used.
rictus: The gape of the mouth, as of birds; -- often resricted to the corners of the mouth.
risibility: The quality of being risible; as, risibility is peculiar to the human species. A strong and obvious disposition to risibility. Sir W. Scott.
righthanded: 1. Using the right hand habitually, or more easily than the left. 2. Having the same direction or course as the movement of the hands of a watch seen in front; -- said of the motion of a revolving object looked at from a given direction. 3. (Zoöl.) Having the whorls rising from left to right; dextral; -- said of spiral shells. See Illust. of Scalaria.
riviere: A necklace of diamonds or other precious stones, esp. one of several strings.
ringwinding: Armature winding in which the wire is wound round the outer and inner surfaces alternately of an annular or cylindrical core.
ribwort: A species of plantain (Plantago lanceolata) with long, narrow, ribbed leaves; -- called also rib grass, ripple grass, ribwort plantain.
ritualist: One skilled un, or attached to, a ritual; one who advocates or practices ritualism.
rightness: Straightness; as, the rightness of a line. Bacon. 2. The quality or state of being right; right relation. The craving for rightness with God. J. C. Shairp.
rima: A narrow and elongated aperture; a cleft; a fissure.
ridgebone: The backbone. (old) Blood . . . lying cluttered about the ridgebone. Holland.
ridgy: Having a ridge or ridges; rising in a ridge. "Lifted on a ridgy wave." Pope.
ricinelaidin: The glycerin salt of ricinelaidic acid, obtained as a white crystalline waxy substance by treating castor oil with nitrous acid.
ringent: Having the lips widely separated and gaping like an open mouth; as a ringent bilabiate corolla.
ride: 1. To be carried on the back of an animal, as a horse. To-morrow, when ye riden by the way. Chaucer. Let your master ride on before, and do you gallop after him. Swift. 2. To be borne in a carriage; | 1. To sit on, so as to be carried; as, to ride a horse; to ride a bicycle. [They] rend up both rocks and hills, and ride the air In whirlwind. Milton. 2. To manage insolently at will;
rigoll: A musical instrument formerly in use, consisting of several sticks bound together, but separated by beads, and played with a stick with a ball at its end. Moore (Encyc. of Music. ).
rider: 1. One who, or that which, rides. 2. Formerly, an agent who went out with samples of goods to obtain orders; a commercial traveler. [Eng.] 3. One who breaks or manages a horse. Shak. 4. An addition or amendment to a manuscript or other document, which is attached on a separate piece of paper;
rimbase: A short cylinder connecting a trunnion with the body of a cannon. See Illust. of Cannon.
ritually: By rites, or by a particular rite.
rist: 3d pers. sing. pres. of Rise, contracted from riseth. Chaucer.
riderless: Having no rider; as, a riderless horse. H. Kingsley.
ripperbill: An act or a bill conferring upon a chief executive, as a governor or mayor, large powers of appointment and removal of heads of departments or other subordinate officials. [Polit. Cant, U. S.]
rifacimento: A remaking or recasting; an adaptation, esp. of a literary work or musical composition.
ripost: 1. In fencing, a return thrust after a parry. 2. A quick and sharp refort; a repartee. J. Morley.
rigor: 1. Rigidity; stiffness. 2. (ed.) A sense of chilliness, with contraction of the skin; a convulsive shuddering or tremor, as in the chill preceeding a fever. Rigor caloris ( Etym: [L., rigor of heat]… | 1. The becoming stiff or rigid; the state of being rigid; rigidity; stiffness; hardness. The rest his look Bound with Gorgonian rigor not to move. Milton. 2. (Med.) See 1st Rigor, 2. 3.
rindy: Having a rind or skin. Ash.
ringworm: A contagious affection of the skin due to the presence of a vegetable parasite, and forming ring-shaped discolored patches covered with vesicles or powdery scales. It occurs either on the body, the face, or the scalp. Different varieties are distinguished as Tinea circinata, Tinea tonsurans, etc., but all are caused by the same parasite (a species of Trichophyton).
rinforzando: Increasing; strengthening; -- a direction indicating a sudden increase of force (abbreviated rf., rfz.) Cf. Forzando, and Sforzando.
rickets: A disease which affects children, and which is characterized by a bulky head, crooked spine and limbs, depressed ribs, enlarged and spongy articular epiphyses, tumid abdomen, and short stature, together with clear and often premature mental faculties. The essential cause of the disease appears to be the nondeposition of earthy salts in the osteoid tissues.
rich: 1. Having an abundance of material possessions; possessed of a large amount of property; well supplied with land, goods, or money; wealthy; opulent; affluent; -- opposed to Ant: poor. "Rich merchants." Chaucer. The rich [person] hath many friends. Prov. xiv. 20. As a thief, bent to unhoard the cash Of some rich burgher. Milton. 2. Hence, in general, well supplied; abounding;
riverside: The side or bank of a river.
rinker: One who skates at a rink. [Colloq.]
rid: imp. & p. p. of Ride, v. i. (old) He rid to the end of the village, where he alighted. Thackeray. | 1. To save; to rescue; to deliver; -- with out of. (old) Deliver the poor and needy; rid them out of the hand of the wicked. Ps. lxxxii. 4. 2. To free; to clear; to disencumber; -- followed by of.
ridgeband: The part of a harness which passes over the saddle, and supports the shafts of a cart; -- called also ridgerope, and ridger. Halliwell.
rival: 1. A person having a common right or privilege with another; a partner. (old) If you do meet Horatio and Marcellus, The rivals of my watch, bid them make haste. Shak. 2. | Having the same pretensions or claims; standing in competition for superiority; as, rival lovers; rival claims or pretensions. The strenuous conflicts and alternate victories of two rival…
rille: One of certain narrow, crooked valleys seen, by aid of the telescope, on the surface of the moon.
rigidity: 1. The quality or state of being rigid; want of pliability; the quality of resisting change of from; the amount of resistance with which a body opposes change of form; -- opposed to flexibility, ductility, malleability, and softness. 2. Stiffness of appearance or manner; want of ease or elegance. Sir H. Wotton. 3. Severity; rigor. [Obs. orR.] Bp. Burnet. Syn. -- Stiffness;
rightangled: Containing a right angle or right angles; as, a right-angled triangle.
ribband: A long, narrow strip of timber bent and bolted longitudinally to the ribs of a vessel, to hold them in position, and give rigidity to the framework. Rib-band lines, oblique longitudinal sectionss of the hull of a vessel. Knight.
rietboc: The reedbuck, a South African antelope (Cervicapra arundinacea); -- so called from its frequenting dry places covered with high grass or reeds. Its color is yellowish brown. Called also inghalla, and rietbok.
rixdollar: A name given to several different silver coins of Denmark, Holland, Sweden,, NOrway, etc., varying in value from about 30 cents to $1.10; also, a British coin worth about 36 cents, used in Ceylon and at the Cape of Good Hope. See Rigsdaler, Riksdaler, and Rixdaler. Note: Most of these pieces are now no longer coined, but some remain in circulation.
riptowel: A gratuity given to tenants after they had reaped their lord's corn. (old)
risorial: Pertaining to, or producing, laughter; as, the risorial muscles.
rissole: A small ball of rich minced meat or fish, covered with pastry and fried.
ribaldry: The talk of a ribald; low, vulgar language; indecency; obscenity; lewdness; -- now chiefly applied to indecent language, but formerly, as by Chaucer, also to indecent acts or conduct. The ribaldry of his conversation moved Macaulay.
ringnecked: Having a well defined ring of color around the neck. Ring- necked duck (Zool.), an American scaup duck (Aythya collaris). The head, neck, and breast of the adult male are black, and a narrow, but conspicuous, red ring encircles the neck. This ring is absent in the female. Called also ring-neck, ring-necked blackhead, ringbill, tufted duck, and black jack.
rissoid: Any one of very numerous species of small spiral gastropods of the genus Rissoa, or family Rissoidæ, found both in fresh and salt water.
riant: Laughing; laughable; exciting gayety; gay; merry; delightful to the view, as a landscape. In such cases the sublimity must be drawn from the other sources, with a strict caution, howewer, against anything light and riant. Burke.
risky: Attended with risk or danger; hazardous. "A risky matter." W. Collins. Generalization are always risky. Lowell.
rifleman: A soldier armed with a rifle.
rightward: Toward the right. Rightward and leftward rise the rocks. Southey.
rightwhale: (a) The bowhead, Arctic, or Greenland whale (Balæna mysticetus), from whose mouth the best whalebone is obtained. (b) Any other whale that produces valuable whalebone, as the Atlantic, or Biscay, right whale (Balæna cisarctica), and the Pacific right whale (B. Sieboldii); a bone whale.
rigmarole: A succession of confused or nonsencial statements; foolish talk; nonsense. [Colloq.] Often one's dear friend talks something which one scruples to call rigmarole. De Quincey. | Consisting of rigmarole; frovolous; nonsensical; foolish.
ringing: a & n. from Ring, v. Ringing engine, a simple form of pile driver in which the monkey is lifted by men pulling on ropes.
rind: The external covering or coat, as of flesh, fruit, trees, etc.; skin; hide; bark; peel; shell. Thou canst not touch the freedom of my mind With all thy charms, although this corporal rind Thou hast… | To remove the rind of; to bark.
riches: 1. That which makes one rich; an abundance of land, goods, money, or other property; wealth; opulence; affluence. Riches do not consist in having more gold and silver, but in having more in proportion, than our neighbors. Locke. 2. That which appears rich, sumptuous, precious, or the like. The riche of heaven's pavement, trodden gold. Milton.
rincon: An interior corner; a nook; hence, an angular recess or hollow bend in a mountain, river, cliff, or the like. [Western & Southern U. S.] D. S. Jordan.
rigger: 1. One who rigs or dresses; one whose occupation is to fit the rigging of a ship. 2. A cylindrical pulley or drum in machinery.
rightly: 1. Straightly; directly; in front. (old) Shak. 2. According to justice; according to the divine will or moral rectitude; uprightly; as, duty rightly performed. 3. Properly; fitly; suitably; appropriately. Eve rightly called, Mother of all mankind. Milton. 4. According to truth or fact; correctly; not erroneously; exactly. "I can not rightly say." Shak.
ringer: 1. One who, or that which, rings; especially, one who rings chimes on bells. 2. (Mining) A crowbar. Simmonds. | A horse that is not entitled to take part in a race, but is fraudulently got into it.
rictal: Of or pertaining to the rictus; as, rictal bristles.
ringbird: The reed bunting. It has a collar of white feathers. Called also ring bunting.
ridable: Suitable for riding; as, a ridable horse; a ridable road.
rife: 1. Prevailing; prevalent; abounding. Before the plague of London, inflammations of the lungs were rife and mortal. Arbuthnot. Even now the tumult of loud mirth Was rife, and perfect in may listening ear. Milton. 2. Having power; active; nimble. (old) What! I am rife a little yet. J. Webster. -- Rife"ly, adv. -- Rife"ness, n.
rindle: A small water course or gutter. Ash.
ritornelle: (a) A short return or repetition; a concluding symphony to an air, often consisting of the burden of the song. (a) A short intermediate symphony, or instrumental passage, in the course of a vocal piece; an interlude.
ridiculous: 1. Fitted to excite ridicule; absurd and laughable; unworthy of serious consideration; as, a ridiculous dress or behavior. Agricola, discerning that those little targets and unwieldy glaives ill pointed would soon become ridiculous against the thrust and close, commanded three Batavian cohorts . . . to draw up and come to handy strokes. Milton. 2.
rie: See Rye. (old) Holland. Rie grass. (Bot.) (a) A kind of wild barley (Hordeum pratense). Dr. Prior. (b) Ray grass. Dr. Prior.
ribbon: 1. A fillet or narrow woven fabric, commonly of silk, used for trimming some part of a woman's attire, for badges, and other decorative purposes. 2. A narrow strip or shred; | To adorn with, or as with, ribbons; to mark with stripes resembling ribbons.
ripple: An implement, with teeth like those of a comb, for removing the seeds and seed vessels from flax, broom corn, etc. | 1. To remove the seeds from (the stalks of flax, etc.), by means of a ripple. 2. Hence, to scratch or tear. Holland.
ris: A bough or branch; a twig. (old) As white as is the blossom upon the ris. Chaucer.
risque: Hazardous; risky; esp., fig., verging upon impropriety; dangerously close to, or suggestive of, what is indecent or of doubtful morality; as, a risqué story. Henry Austin.
ribbing: An assemblage or arrangement of ribs, as the timberwork for the support of an arch or coved ceiling, the veins in the leaves of some plants, ridges in the fabric of cloth, or the like.
rixdaler: A Dutch silver coin, worth about $1.00.
ringbill: The ring-necked scaup duck; -- called also ring-billed blackhead. See Scaup.
rigafir: A species of pine (Pinus sylvestris), and its wood, which affords a valuable timber; -- called also Scotch pine, and red or yellow deal. It grows in all parts of Europe, in the Caucasus, and in Siberia.
ringmaster: One in charge of the performances (as of horses) within the ring in a circus.
ripieno: Filling up; supplementary; supernumerary; -- a term applied to those instruments which only swell the mass or tutti of an orchestra, but are not obbligato.
rib: 1. (Anat.) One of the curved bones attached to the vertebral column and supporting the lateral walls of the thorax. Note: In man there are twelve ribs on each side, of which the upper seven are… | 1. To furnish with ribs; to form with rising lines and channels; as, to rib cloth. 2. To inclose, as with ribs, and protect; to shut in. It [lead] were too gross To rib her cerecloth in the obscure…
rile: 1. To render turbid or muddy; to stir up; to roil. 2. To stir up in feelings; to make angry; to vex. Note: In both senses provincial in England and colloquial in the United States.
rickrack: A kind of openwork edging made of serpentine braid.
rivose: Marked with sinuate and irregular furrows.
rigol: A circle; hence, a diadem. (old) Shak.
ricinelaidic: Pertaining to, or designating, an isomeric modification of ricinoleic acid obtained as a white crystalline solid.
risk: 1. Hazard; danger; peril; exposure to loss, injury, or destruction. The imminent and constant risk of assassination, a risk which has shaken very strong nerves. Macaulay. 2. (Com.) Hazard of loss; | 1. To expose to risk, hazard, or peril; to venture; as, to risk goods on board of a ship; to risk one's person in battle; to risk one's fame by a publication. 2. To incur the risk or danger of;
ridicule: 1. An object of sport or laughter; a laughingstock; a laughing matter. [Marlborough] was so miserably ignorant, that his deficiencies made him the ridicule of his contemporaries. Buckle. | To laugh at mockingly or disparagingly; to awaken ridicule toward or respecting. I 've known the young, who ridiculed his rage. Goldsmith. Syn. -- To deride; banter; rally; burlesque; mock; satirize;
righteousness: 1. The quality or state of being righteous; holiness; purity; uprightness; rectitude. Note: Righteousness, as used in Scripture and theology, in which it chiefly occurs, is nearly equivalent to holiness, comprehending holy principles and affections of heart, and conformity of life to the divine law. 2. A righteous act, or righteous quality.
riflebird: Any one of several species of beautiful birds of Australia and New Guinea, of the genera Ptiloris and Craspidophora, allied to the paradise birds. Note: The largest and best known species is Ptiloris paradisea of Australia. Its general color is rich velvety brown, glossed with lilac;
ribibe: 1. A sort of stringed instrument; a rebec. (old) Nares. 2. An old woman; -- in contempt. (old) Chaucer. 3. A bawd; a prostitute. (old) B. Jonson.
ringed: 1. Encircled or marked with, or as with, a ring or rings. 2. Wearning a wedding ring; hence, lawfully wedded. "A ringed wife." Tennyson. Ringed seal (Zoöl.), a North Pacific seal (Phoca foetida) having ringlike spots on the body. -- Ringed snake (Zoöl.), a harmless European snake (Tropidonotus natrix) common in England. -- Ringed worm (Zoöl.), an annelid.
rice: A well-known cereal grass (Oryza sativa) and its seed. This plant is extensively cultivated in warm climates, and the grain forms a large portion of the food of the inhabitants. In America it grows chiefly on low, moist land, which can be overflowed. Ant rice. (Bot.) See under Ant. -- French rice. (Bot.) See Amelcorn.
